items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider the following system of linear equations:
[MATH: {x_{1} + x_{2} = − 2; − x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 4; 2x_{1} − x_{2} = 2]

Content:
It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system.

Content:
Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form [MATH: A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [1|1; − 1|− 4; 2|− 1]]

Content:
We are interested in vectors [MATH: \hat{\mathbf{x}}] such that [MATH: A\hat{\mathbf{x}}] is very close to [MATH: \mathbf b.] More precisely, we wish to minimize the distance between [MATH: A\hat{\mathbf{x}}] and [MATH: \mathbf b.] Recall that the distance between [MATH: A\hat{\mathbf{x}}] and [MATH: \mathbf b] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \Vert A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.]

Content:
The smaller the value of [MATH: \Vert A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,] the better our approximation [MATH: \hat{\mathbf{x}}] will be.

Content:
In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] that lies in [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A)] and is closest to [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]
Therefore, [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] must be the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{b}] onto the subspace spanned by the columns of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a9d0b2b43fd73bf698e36b97875d410]

Content:
It can be shown that [MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] is found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by
[MATH: A^{T}Ax^(^)|= A^{T}b.]

Content:
We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation [MATH: A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b] by [MATH: A^T.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: A^T \! A] is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by [MATH: (A^T \! A)^{-1},] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
We now compute the right-hand side as follows:
[MATH: x^(^)|= (A^{T}A)^{− 1}A^{T}b; = ([1|− 1|2; 1|− 4|− 1][1|1; − 1|− 4; 2|− 1])^{− 1}[1|− 1|2; 1|− 4|− 1][− 2; 4; 2]; = [6|3; 3|18]^{− 1}[− 2; − 20]; = (1)/(99)[18|− 3; − 3|6][− 2; − 20]; = [(8)/(33); − (38)/(33)]]

Content:
The vector [MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] is called the least-squares solution of the given system.

Content:
Watch out! We assumed that the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, which guarantees that [MATH: A^T \! A\,] is invertible. However, if the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly dependent, then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem.

sections.normalized_html: Consider the system [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}], where the matrix [MATH: A] and the vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are given below. Given that the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, find the minimum value of [MATH: \Vert A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.] [MATH: [1|1; 1|0; − 1|0; − 1|− 1]]

Consider the system [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}], where the matrix [MATH: A] and the vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are given below. Given that the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, find the minimum value of [MATH: \Vert A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.]
[MATH: [1|1; 1|0; − 1|0; − 1|− 1]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First of all, we write the given system in the form [MATH: A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [1|1; 1|0; − 1|0; − 1|− 1]^(⏞)^(A)[x_{1}; x_{2}]^(⏞)^(x)|= [22; 0; 0; 2]^(⏞)^(b); Ax|= b]

We can find the least-squares solution [MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by [MATH: A^T\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: A^{T}Ax^(^)|= A^{T}b]

Since the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: A^T \! A] is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by [MATH: (A^T \! A)^{-1}] on the left, we obtain

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's consider the following system of linear equations:
[MATH: {x_{1} + x_{2} = − 2; − x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 4; 2x_{1} − x_{2} = 2]

Content:
It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system.

Content:
Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form [MATH: A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [1|1; − 1|− 4; 2|− 1]]

Content:
We are interested in vectors [MATH: \hat{\mathbf{x}}] such that [MATH: A\hat{\mathbf{x}}] is very close to [MATH: \mathbf b.] More precisely, we wish to minimize the distance between [MATH: A\hat{\mathbf{x}}] and [MATH: \mathbf b.] Recall that the distance between [MATH: A\hat{\mathbf{x}}] and [MATH: \mathbf b] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \Vert A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.]

Content:
The smaller the value of [MATH: \Vert A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,] the better our approximation [MATH: \hat{\mathbf{x}}] will be.

Content:
In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] that lies in [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A)] and is closest to [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]
Therefore, [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] must be the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{b}] onto the subspace spanned by the columns of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a9d0b2b43fd73bf698e36b97875d410]

Content:
It can be shown that [MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] is found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by
[MATH: A^{T}Ax^(^)|= A^{T}b.]

Content:
We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation [MATH: A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b] by [MATH: A^T.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: A^T \! A] is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by [MATH: (A^T \! A)^{-1},] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
We now compute the right-hand side as follows:
[MATH: x^(^)|= (A^{T}A)^{− 1}A^{T}b; = ([1|− 1|2; 1|− 4|− 1][1|1; − 1|− 4; 2|− 1])^{− 1}[1|− 1|2; 1|− 4|− 1][− 2; 4; 2]; = [6|3; 3|18]^{− 1}[− 2; − 20]; = (1)/(99)[18|− 3; − 3|6][− 2; − 20]; = [(8)/(33); − (38)/(33)]]

Content:
The vector [MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] is called the least-squares solution of the given system.

Content:
Watch out! We assumed that the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly independent, which guarantees that [MATH: A^T \! A\,] is invertible. However, if the columns of [MATH: A] are linearly dependent, then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem.

Item 11 — Tutorial: Deriving the Normal Equation

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: A] is an [MATH: m \times n] matrix with linearly independent columns. We'll now explain why the least-squares solution [MATH: {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] to the least-squares problem

Content:
[MATH: A\mathbf x = \mathbf b]

Content:
can be found by solving the normal equation
[MATH: A^{T}Ax^(^)|= A^{T}b.]

Content:
The vector [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}] must be the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{b}] onto the subspace spanned by the columns of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a5d508e71c2b7ab3ba2ec4e3b3d86e38]

Content:
As a result, we have that

Content:
[MATH: (A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}) \perp \textrm{Col}(A),]

Content:
which is equivalent to saying that [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}] is orthogonal to each column [MATH: \mathbf{a}_i] of [MATH: A.] Thus, the dot product of the columns of [MATH: A] and the vector [MATH: A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}] must be equal to [MATH: 0{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {a_{1}^{T}(Ax^(^) − b) = 0; a_{2}^{T}(Ax^(^) − b) = 0; ⋮; a_{n}^{T}(Ax^(^) − b) = 0]

Content:
This system of equations can be written in terms of matrix products as

Content:
[MATH: A^T (A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Finally, expanding the left-hand side, we obtain our normal equation:

Content:
[MATH: A^{T}(Ax^(^) − b)|= 0; A^{T}Ax^(^) − A^{T}b|= 0; A^{T}Ax^(^)|= A^{T}b]
